sentences: Between Elizabeth and Charlotte there was a restraint which kept them mutually silent on the subject; and Elizabeth felt persuaded that no real confidence could ever subsist between them again.

senses.gloss: discipline in personal and social activities
senses.learner: Control over yourself in what you do on your own and with other people.
examples: He showed great restraint and did not shout back.

senses.gloss: a rule or condition that limits freedom
senses.learner: A rule or condition that limits how free you are.
examples: The new law put restraints on how much the banks could lend.

senses.gloss: the act of controlling by restraining someone or something
senses.learner: The act of controlling someone or something by holding them back.
examples: The small shops suffered from the restraint of trade by the big companies.

senses.gloss: the state of being physically constrained
senses.learner: The state of being held so that you cannot move freely.
examples: The prisoner was kept under restraint.

senses.gloss: lack of ornamentation
senses.learner: The quality of having little or no decoration.
examples: The room was decorated with great restraint, with plain white walls.

senses.gloss: a device that retards something's motion
senses.learner: A device that slows down or holds back the movement of something.
examples: The child was held in the seat by a safety restraint.

senses.gloss: the physical magnitude of something (how big it is)
senses.learner: How big or small something is.
examples: You ought to make some kind of remark on the size of the room, or the number of couples.

senses.gloss: a large magnitude
senses.learner: The fact of being big.
examples: He went pale when he saw the size of the bill.
It is the only town of any size in that area.

senses.gloss: the property resulting from being one of a series of graduated measurements (as of clothing)
senses.learner: Which one of a set of fixed, graded measures something is, as with clothes.
examples: She wears a size 8 dress.

senses.gloss: the actual state of affairs
senses.learner: The way things really are.
examples: He lost his job, and that's about the size of it.

senses.gloss: any glutinous material used to fill pores in surfaces or to stiffen fabrics

examples: The painter brushed size onto the wall before hanging the paper.

senses.gloss: speaking of yourself in superlatives

Mr. Darcy's shameful boast of what misery he had been able to inflict gave her a keener sense of her sister's sufferings.

sentences: It was dated from Rosings, at eight o'clock in the morning, and was as follows:--

The beginning contained an account of all their little parties and engagements, with such news as the country afforded; but the latter half, which was dated a day later, and written in evident agitation, gave more important intelligence.
"It has been coming on so gradually, that I hardly know when it began; but I believe I must date it from my first seeing his beautiful grounds at Pemberley."

senses.gloss: provide with a dateline; mark with a date
senses.learner: To write a line on something giving its date, or simply to mark it with a date.
examples: It was dated from Rosings, at eight o'clock in the morning.
The latter half, which was dated a day later, gave more important intelligence.

senses.gloss: assign a date to; determine the (probable) date of
senses.learner: To give something a date, or to work out when it most likely happened or was made.
examples: I believe I must date it from my first seeing his beautiful grounds at Pemberley.

senses.gloss: go on a date with
senses.learner: To go out with someone on a planned romantic meeting.
examples: He dated her once, but they never met again.

senses.gloss: date regularly; have a steady relationship with
senses.learner: To go out with someone regularly and have a steady romantic relationship with them.
examples: They have been dating for two years.

senses.gloss: stamp with a date
senses.learner: To press a stamp showing the date onto something.
examples: The clerk dated each form with a rubber stamp.

sentences: They found Mary, as usual, deep in the study of thorough bass and human nature; and had some new extracts to admire and some new observations of threadbare morality to listen to.

senses.gloss: to a great depth; far down or in
senses.learner: A long way down or a long way in.
examples: They dug deep to find water.

senses.gloss: to a great distance
senses.learner: A long distance.
examples: The soldiers pushed deep into enemy land.

senses.gloss: to an advanced time
senses.learner: Until a late point in time.
examples: They talked deep into the night.

sentences: Mrs. Bennet deigned not to make any reply; but, unable to contain herself, began scolding one of her daughters.

senses.gloss: do something that one considers to be below one's dignity
senses.learner: To do something even though you think it is beneath you.
examples: Mr. Wickham touched his hat--a salutation which Mr. Darcy just deigned to return.
Mrs. Bennet deigned not to make any reply.

senses.gloss: guide or conduct or usher somewhere
senses.learner: To guide or lead someone to a place.
examples: Mr. Darcy handed the ladies into the carriage.
He then handed her in, Maria followed.

senses.gloss: place into the hands or custody of
senses.learner: To put something into someone's hands or into their care.
examples: Please hand me the spoon.
